Narcissus
nar-SIS-us
proper noun
Greek Narkissos, the name of a flower; a man of Rome whose household held believers in the Lord.

📖 Biblical Definition

Narcissus is named once in Scripture, in the greetings of the sixteenth chapter of Romans: “Greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord” (Rom 16:11). It is worthy of careful note that Paul does not greet Narcissus himself, but only those of his household who are “in the Lord.” Narcissus was a wealthy Roman name, borne by a famous freedman of the emperor Claudius; whether this be the same man or another, the master of the house appears not to have been a believer. Yet within his household — among his servants, freedmen, and dependents — there were those who belonged to Christ, a little company of saints gathered under the roof of an unbelieving lord. Paul singles them out with tender care: not all the household, but “them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.” Here is a sweet and humbling picture of the early church: bondservants and lowly men, set in great households not their own, yet partakers of a liberty their masters knew not. Narcissus, or rather his household, stands as a witness that the grace of God springs up in the most unlikely soil; that the Lord has His own hidden in the houses of the great and the worldly; and that Christ knows each of His own by name, even the servant in an unbelieving master’s house.

A man of Rome whose household held believers; Paul greets “them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord” (Rom 16:11).

Paul greets those of his household “which are in the Lord.”

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:11 — "Salute Herodion my kinsman. Greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord."

Rom 16:10 — "Salute Apelles approved in Christ. Salute them which are of Aristobulus' household."

1Co 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:"

Php 4:22 — "All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A saint of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his household witnesses that grace springs up even in unbelieving houses.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the grace of God springs up in the most unlikely soil. Paul greets not Narcissus, who seems no believer, but those of his household “which are in the Lord” — a little company of saints, likely servants and freedmen, gathered under the roof of an unbelieving lord. The Lord has His own hidden in the houses of the great and the worldly, partakers of a liberty their masters know not.

The careful words “which are in the Lord” also witness that Christ knows His own by name and distinguishes them from all others. Not the whole household, but those in the Lord, are greeted; the Spirit marks the difference between the merely outward members of a house and the true members of Christ’s body. So the saints scattered in worldly households are known and named by their Saviour, and remembered by His apostle, though the world overlook them as the lowest of servants.
